dct_description_sm: The Land Surface Temperature (LST) is one of the most important parameters required to map and monitor many environmental phenomena, such as surface energy balances (Park et al. 2005, Intl. J. Rem. Sens 26:6), global and regional climates (Comiso, 2003, J. Climate 16, Yu et al., 2008, IEEE Trans. Geosci. Rem. Sens. 46:1), inland water bodies (Schneider and Hook, 2010, Geoph. Res. Lett. L22405), vegetation density (Julien and Sobrino, 2009, Rem. Sens. of Env. 113), and permafrost temperature regime (Marchenko et al., 2009, Geophy.l Res. Abstracts, 11, EGU11077). Retrieved from satellite sensors which cover large swaths of terrain at a highly repeated frequency, LSTs offer an appropriate answer to the problem of inconsistent coverage due to missing spatial data. In Arctic and Subarctic regions, meteorological stations are scattered across the territory and poorly distributed geographically. There is therefore a need for a method to measure and to map surface temperature, or to support regional interpolations, in order to improve the appraisal of climate conditions across the vast areas between stations. Repeated space borne mapping of surface temperatures year after year also provides a mean to monitor climate variations at a high spatial resolution. The LSTs from satellites were used to develop Canadas maps of monthly and annual near-surface temperatures (Tm), as well as of freezing (Fi) and thawing (Ti) indices.
dct_title_s: Land Surface Temperature maps over Canada
